title: Strictly Local Tile-Code Architectures on Two-Dimensional Planar Lattices
abstract: Tile codes are a family of planar quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with weight-6 stabilizers and open boundary conditions, offering an encoding efficiency $kd^2/n$ of up to four times that of the surface code. In this work, we develop an exhaustive search algorithm for finding SWAP-based routing schemes that implement syndrome extraction for four tile-code families using only nearest-neighbor interactions on a two-dimensional square lattice, matching the connectivity of the surface code. Using explicitly constructed routed syndrome-extraction circuits decoded with BP+OSD, we estimate the circuit-level thresholds of these code families. For the SI1000 noise model, the threshold without such a connectivity constraint is obtained in a range 0.23%-0.31%, while it decreases to 0.11%-0.13% with routing, representing a reduction factor of around two to three. Despite this threshold penalty, our resource-footprint analysis shows that routed tile codes require fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than the surface code at sufficiently low physical error rates: Under the SI1000 noise model, we find a crossover near $p^*\approx 0.08\%$, below which routed tile codes become more qubit-efficient, with an advantage that grows monotonically as the physical error rate decreases.
summary: This paper analyzes Tile Codes for fault-tolerant quantum computation on 2D lattices, focusing on implementing syndrome extraction using only local interactions. By developing optimized routing schemes, they show that while locality imposes a threshold penalty, the resulting codes offer superior qubit efficiency compared to surface codes at low physical error rates. The work validates planar qLDPC codes as a viable alternative for near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop and analyze strictly local Tile-Code Architectures for fault-tolerant quantum computation on 2D planar lattices, seeking to improve encoding efficiency over the surface code.
main_result: Routing syndrome extraction circuits significantly reduces the error threshold of tile codes when nearest-neighbor connectivity is enforced. Furthermore, routed tile codes become more qubit-efficient than the surface code below a critical physical error rate ($p^* \approx 0.08\%$).
method: The authors developed an exhaustive search algorithm for SWAP-based routing schemes to implement syndrome extraction circuits and compared performance using various decoding algorithms like BP+OSD.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Tile Codes, a family of planar quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, implemented on a two-dimensional square lattice. The analysis involves simulating error correction under the SI1000 noise model and standard depolarizing noise.
key_observables: Circuit-level thresholds ($p_{th}$), resource footprint (physical qubits per logical qubit), and logical error rate ($p_L$) vs. physical error rate ($p$).
important_parameters: The encoding efficiency $kd^2/n$, the crossover physical error rate $p^* \approx 0.08\%$, and the noise model parameters (SI1000).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that SWAP gates are native operations, and optimal routing schedules are found within a specific class of uniform SWAP direction assignments.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate code constructions on lattices, compare $p_L$ vs. $p$ for different decoders (e.g., BP+OSD vs. others), and show the resource efficiency comparison between routed tile codes and surface codes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the local architecture and developing routing schemes; it then analyzes the resulting circuit-level thresholds under noise models; finally, it compares decoding performance across multiple algorithms and assesses qubit resource efficiency against established codes like the surface code.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, hardware-aware comparisons of quantum error correcting codes, directly addressing the practical constraints (like nearest-neighbor connectivity) that limit theoretical proposals in superconducting or solid-state quantum computing platforms.

Within each panel, lighter shades indicate smaller code distances (see Table I). Dashed vertical lines indicate the threshold for each family obtained from the finite-size scaling.

Four decoding algorithms are compared: BP+OSD, BP+LSD, BP+UFD (BeliefFind), and MWPF. All BP-based decoders use the same front-end (min-sum, scaling factor 0.5, max 2000 iterations).
